The Night Ferry’s Quiet Return

A shuttered river ferry is sailing again, and a bookshop has moved aboard.

By Alex Reporter — March 17, 2024

On the first Saturday of spring, a small crowd gathered at the old pier in Eastmere to watch a white ferry that had not moved in six years pull away from the dock. Its lower deck, once lined with benches, now holds Harbor Lights Books, a shop of about four thousand titles that sails the river every evening. 

More than three hundred passengers boarded that night, paying the usual fare, browsing the shelves between stops, and staying on for the return trip because, as one of them put it, the last chapter was not finished yet.

“It is a reading room that happens to float,” said Casey Placeholder, a retired pilot who steered the same boat for twenty years before the service was cancelled. “People used to sleep on this route. Now they argue about novels.” 

The ferry line closed when a new bridge opened downstream, and the boat sat in a repair yard, its paint peeling, its engine drained. The town council, the operator, and a group of neighbours spent two years negotiating a lease, and the shop opened with borrowed shelving and a donated till.

The idea belongs to Robin Sample, a former schoolteacher who ran a stall at the Eastmere market for a decade. Sample says the ferry offered what a storefront could not: a captive audience, a view, and a reason to linger for forty minutes at a time.

“On land, people come in, look around, and leave,” Sample said. “On the water, they cannot leave until the next stop, so they read the first page, and then the second, and then they buy the book.”

The shop keeps its stock small and seasonal. There are maps of the river, cookbooks from the towns along its banks, a shelf of poetry chosen by passengers, and a box of paperbacks that anyone may borrow for the length of a crossing, provided they leave it on board.

A ferry is the only place in town where strangers agree to sit still together. The books just give them something to talk about.

Jordan Example, a regular commuter on the evening route

Not everyone was convinced at first. Some residents worried about noise, some about parking at the pier, and a few simply thought a bookshop would never pay. The operator agreed to a one-year trial, with the council reviewing ticket numbers every quarter.

The numbers so far are encouraging. Evening sailings are running close to full on weekends, weekday trips carry a steady crowd of commuters, and the shop has started hosting readings on the upper deck, where the wind makes microphones a necessity.

Sample is already planning a winter timetable, with shorter crossings, heavier blankets, and a larger shelf of long novels. “The river does not close in winter,” she said, “and neither will we.”

Alex Reporter is a staff writer for The Example Wire.
